The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 193) to amend the Public Works Act. He said : Under the Public Works Act it is provided that the department shall invite tenders for all work to be done. But for the last twenty years, under an Order in Council and on the discretion of the minister, the department could do work up to the amount of $5,000 without inviting tenders. That Order in Council, I understand, has been declared ultra vires by an opinion of the Department of Justice. It is my intention to ask that the Act be amended so as to provide that the department can expend sums up to the amount of $5,000 without inviting tenders ; in other words, making legal by legislation what has been the custom for a great many years in the department.

speechtext: 1. Has an investigation been made in regard to the accumulation of postal matter in the Montreal post office ?

2.	By whom was said investigation made ?
3.	What is the result of said investigation ?
4.	Did the person charged with said investigation hear any of the employees upon whom devolves the duty of handling said mail matter?

If it is intended by this Question to suggest that there has been any accumulation of general postal matter in the Montreal post office, such a suggestion is without foundation. The history of the post office shows that at leading city post offices, on exceptional occasions, large quantities of printed, circular and other advertising matter, at times amounting to tons in weight, are at the same moment delivered at the post office for distribution, but such matter is not allowed to interfere with the regular despatch of ordinary regular mail matter. One such instance occurred at Montreal a few weeks ago, owing to the unexpected arrival at that point of a considerable quantity of American circulars, advertisements and sample newspapers, and was in due course disposed of without any interruption whatever to the despatch of the regular business of the office.
No formal investigation was called for or held. It happened that a certain newspaper in Montreal charged the department with delay in the transmission of mail matter, and the Chief Post Office Superintendent, being in Montreal at the time, looked into the matter and informed himself by inquiry of the proper officers as to what foundation there was for the charge, and he found the facts to be as above stated.

It seems to me that in the latter part of the section there is some confusion of language. You say that:
Every document purporting to he signed by the chief commissioner and secretary, or by either of them, shall be prima facie evidence in all courts.

On section 29,
The company shall, as soon as possible after the receipt by it, or service upon it, of any regulation, order, direction, decision, notice, report or other document of the hoard, or the minister, or the Inspecting engineer, give cognizance thereof to each of its officers and servants performing duties which are or may be affected thereby, by delivering a copy to him or by posting up a copy thereof in some place where his work or his duties, or some of them, are to be performed. 51 V., c. 29, s. 25, Am.

I would suggest to the hon. minister that the words in the section, after the word ' thereby ' be struck out, and some words like these inserted : ' And shall see that such regulation, order, &c., Is properly carried out.' You are limiting the company to a certain way of delivering the document, and I think it would be move practicable to leave it to the company themselves to decide the best way of reaching their servants or employees, so long as they carried it out. I submit thatjfor the consideration of the minister.

There were a number of suggestions made by some Ontario organizations, -boards of trade or town councils-and this may be one of them. Some of these sug-

gestions, it was not thought well, ou consideration, to adopt, because they were framed without a knowledge of the scheme of the Bill as a whole. On a superficial glance, they might seem to he all right, while if adopted they would dislocate some parts of the Bill. On section 39,
When any work, act, matter or thing is, by any regulation, order or decision of the board, required to be done, performed or completed within a specified time, the board may, if the circumstances of the case seem to so require, upon notice and hearing, or in its discretion, upon ex-parte application, extend the time so specified.

Is that not a little dangerous to suggest that they may in their discretion, extend that time without hearing the other party ? They might be interfering with the other party's rights. There is no objection to their having the power to extend the time, but there is a danger that they might interfere with the rights of the other party if they are allowed to extend the time in their discretion on an ex parte application.	,

A sudden emergency might arise where it might be necessary to extend the time without giving notice, and where it would be undesirable to hamper them in the exercise of their discretion. It is well to make the Act as elastic as possible. We do not want to see the commission brought up standing against some legislative obstacle, as they might be if they are not given discretion. Circumstances may occur which would make it in the highest degree necessary to ail parties that a moderate extension of time should be allowed. On section 41,
No order of the board need show upon its face that any proceeding or notice was had or given, or any circumstance existed, necessary to give it jurisdiction to make such order.

Should not an ex parte application or order say that it is an ex parte one ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. I do not think it is necessary to

require that that should be done in order to give the commission jurisdiction. This is a class of legislation which is very much adopted in order to avoid the possibility of acts of the tribunal being set aside.

It may not be necessary to make the order show all the circumstances that are required to exist to give jurisdiction, but it would be right to have the order say whether it was given on notice or ex parte. I think my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is right. The order should state whether it is made ex parte or 6n notice.

I think where it would be ex parte we may be safe in assuming that there will be no likelihood of omitting the statement, but I would not like to put it in the statute. There are a large number of cases in which it is provided that ex parte orders may be made temporarily, made only to enable time to elapse so that notice to the other side may be given. It is hardly well to encumber the Bill too much or to assume that any reasonable statement of the reason for making the order would not be there.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My point is this; I am not saying that the statute should say that notice must be given or that the order must say that it is ex parte or not. If the section read in this way it would be better :
No order of the board need show upon its face that any circumstance existed, necessary to give it jurisdiction to make such order.
It need not say whether notice was or was not given, but if you leave in the words ' any proceeding or notice ' you are almost enacting that the board shall not say that the order was made on notice. You are rather indicating to them that it would be better not to do so. You are legislating on a matter that is all right from the hon. minister's contention, if these words are left out. By leaving these words in, we give notice to the commission that they should not say in their order whether it has been issued oil notice or ex parte. I think they should be free to do so.

I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman is wrong in saying that any inference of that kind will be drawn by persons administering this Act. There will be no purpose served by setting forth in the order whether it was made ex parte or not, because the people who are interested and who claim that they ought to have had notice before any order was made would know whether it had been or not. They need not be acquainted with what is already within their own knowledge. It is not necessary to assert that the order was issued with or without notice in order to give jurisdiction. The fact of the notice is not necessarily an element in jurisdiction, because the Bill provides that temporarily
and in emergencies interim orders may lie made ex parte and this is regarded as likely to be necessary in many cases. You cannot reach people to give them notice. Some emergency may arise and the board ought to have power to act without notice.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is a different question.

No, it is not a different thing. Therefore, notice to the party would not be necessarily an element in jurisdiction in many cases. We are only dealing with the question of jurisdiction. We are only providing that the jurisdiction shall not be questioned because of the omission to allege or set forth any circumstances which existed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would not that be sufficient without expressly saying ' any proceeding or notice was had or given ? '

It refers to the circumstances existing in the case relating to the merits. It is not the circumstance as to who made the application or who was present at the time tiie order was made. If the presence or absence of notice is necessary to constitute jurisdiction, then, it would be necessary to allege it in every case. It could not lie alleged truthfully in every case, and it would not be necessary in every case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not mean that it should be necessary to allege that there was notice given, and that if the parties got notice that is all there would be about it. The party who got the notice or did not might want to prove that he had the notice or he had not as the case might be. A party might want to be able to prove that it was an ex parte order, and I think he should be allowed to. The order would prove in the hands of anybody whether .it was an ex parte order or an order on notice, and I think it would be well that it should do so.

On section 50, subsection 2,
No person shall be excused from attending and testifying or from producing books, papers, tariffs, contracts, agreements and documents before the board, or in obedience to the subpoena or order of the board, or of any rerson

authorized to hold any investigation or inquiry under this Act, or in any cause or proceeding based upon or growing out of any alleged violation of this Act, on the ground or for the reason that the testimony or evidence, documentary or otherwise, required of him, may tend to criminate or subject him to a penalty under this Act.

speechtext: I think there ought to be here a provision like that in the Criminal Code with regard to protecting a man if he gives the evidence. Under this section, you might make a man criminate himself. But, in such a case sufficient public benefit is gained by his evidence and you .should give him the protection afforded by the Criminal Code. The exact words of the criminal law on this point I have not at hand at the moment. But they have been found to work out very well. They provide that a man is bound to attend and give evidence, but, if he gives the evidence, he is absolved from criminal prosecution except prosecution for perjury in relation to the evidence he gives. I do not think it would be well, as a matter of public policy, to leave the section as it is here. Under this section a man might be compelled virtually to put a halter around his own neck and lock himself up. In that case he is apt not to tell the truth. But, if he is freed from a criminal prosecution, you can probably get from him, all the facts, and that is what is needed in the public interest. I should suggest that the bon. gentleman insert here the words of the Criminal Code with regard to a similar state of affairs.

I intended to propose an amendment which may be in line with what the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster) suggests. I move to strike out the words ' a penalty under this Act ' at the end of the clause, and to put in their place the following : ' any proceeding or penalty, but no evidence so given or any document so produced shall be used or received against such person in any criminal proceeding thereafter instituted against him, other than prosecution for perjury in giving such evidence.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose that this point has been very carefully considered. It is covered in the Canada Evidence Act, I think, and I suppose, in the code also. Are we following the same language ?

The Finance Minister intended to look into this Bill.
_ The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding). I have made some inquiries. The hon. member who has charge of the Bill will be able to explain the points involved.

The purpose of this Bill was merely to extend the time of this particular insurance company. But the Department of Finance requested the promoters of the Bill to make some changes by which the powers of the company were limited instead of extended. These changes were agreed to, and the Bill was passed by the committee about a week ago. One or two other clauses were added also, one to enable the company to change its name, because the present name is very like the name of another company in existence. The Bill passed through the committee without any opposition.

One of the questions raised was in reference to whether or not the somewhat elaborate sections introduced by way of amendments were covered by the notice given of the Bill in the ' Canada Gazette ' and the local press. That is a matter which perhaps would not come to the attention of the committee to which the Bill is referred and, of course, the Committee on Standing Orders would only have regard to the provisions of the Bill as originally introduced. Is there anything in tli0 amendments which would fairly require further notice ?

I do not know how that would be technically, but I think there is no need of anything of that kind. As I say, the amend-Mr. McCREARY.
ments proposed in the committee deprived the company of some powers which they held under the old charter.

Where a Bill is introduced in conformity with the notice, the House claims the right to change it if necessary. I do not think there is anything in the rule which would prevent our considering it. Of course, if the changes were very material, it would be a fair argument that notice should be given so that the parties concerned should be protected. I was not present at the consideration of this Bill, but I am informed that officers of my department were present and were satisfied with it, and no doubt, taking that statement, it was well considered. Personally, I was not present, nor did I hear the discussion.

I think we would have to take these suggestions with a little caution, because otherwise a very important measure might go through the House with very little notice. speechtext: Why should the company pay back to a shareholder who has put his money into the concern, part of that money pending the completion of the railway ? I have no doubt there must be some plausible reason for it which was urged when it was originally passed, but I am rather at a loss to conceive what that reason could have been ?

The only reason that occurs to my mind is that in the initial stages of these undertakings and organizations it is very important to offer considerable inducements to people to subscribe and pay up their stock. I presume it has grown to be a practice, and having become a practice has been consecrated by legislative enactment, and the law has been passed to allow people who have put their money into an undertaking of that kind which cannot possibly be a paying one at the outset, to receive interest upon the money which they have advanced, and from the date at which they have advanced it. I do know, from personal knowledge, having had some little acquaintance with the manner in which companies are financed and organized, that this is not an uncommon thing for other companies to do.

speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman's explanation is just what has taken place in these companies. If the money could not be obtained upon shares during construction, the company would probably have to borrow from banks and pay interest, and they therefore induce shareholders to pay up as early as possible under the promise of getting interest. While it appears an extraordinary thing to pay dividends not earned, yet if the shareholders did not pay up early, and during construction, when the company could not possibly earn any dividends, the company would have to borrow from bondholders or bankers and others and pay interest. I do not know that it wolud make any appreciable difference to the company.
They could make calls payable as the directors might see fit.
Subject to the approval of the shareholders.

But the shareholders, by postponing calls and working the

matter out under this section, would really get back part of the money they put into the company as capital. If you had a railway which occupied a long time to complete, you might have 25 or 30 per cent of the capital paid back to the shareholders by way of interest under this section. I do not regard the principle of the legislation as good, and as far as other companies are concerned, I do not know how any other company could do that legally except by virtue of some such statute as this. Apply it to the case of an ordinary commercial company and see how badly it will work out.
It is done all the same.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If it is done the directors are subjecting themselves probably to a criminal prosecution. They are putting themselves exactly in the same position as they would place themselves if they paid dividends out of capital.
This is only during construction.

This is only during construction, but a railway takes a very long time to construct and it is different in that respect from the working of any other undertaking. In the latter case the operation begins almost at once. The operation of a railway may be postponed for a long time, and during that time the slmre-[DOT] holders cannot get any dividends out of profits, because no profits cS.n be earned. It seems to me that the better way is to leave this out. Any man who goes into the business of a railway knows when he has put in his money that he cannot get a return for four or five years. He is in no worse position than the man who puts his money into a life assurance company, and who knows that he cannot get dividends for five or six years. I cannot see very much distinction between allowing a life assurance company to pay dividends out of capital and allowing railway companies to pay dividends out of capital. However this may be sanctioned by practice and the fact that it is already on the statute-book, I am bound to say -that I cannot approve of the principle of it.

Here is the principle of it:	Where a subsidy of so much
per mile is given upon the completion of a road, the company hypothecate government securities and sometimes make an arrangement with the government by which the government become the trustees of the fund and one of the conditions of the trust is that pending the completion of the road dividends shall be paid out to the shareholders on the moneys they paid in.

I would not think of introducing a clause into the Bill embodying that principle if it were not there, and yet I feel re-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
luctant to suggest that it should be dropped out. There are many reasons against it, it is true.

These people never pay a cent in cash upon their stock, and the objection I see to this clause is that shareholders who never paid a dollar might be able to draw dividends during construction. isting law and it starts out by the use of language which does not seem to contemplate the idea of a company making a note for borrowing on its credit, but rather suggests that it may simply have power to transfer the note it may receive. speechtext: This clause supersedes any powers given for the construction of the road and any limitation of time provided in any special Act ?
No, the special Act governs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would that be perfectly clear if the special Act had been passed before the enactment of the general Act ?

Section 3 provides for the ease of any special Act passed previous to this Act as follows
If in any special Act heretofore passed by the parliament of Canada it is enacted that any provision of the general Railway Act in force at the time of the passing of such special Act, is expected from incorporation therewith, or if the application of any such provision is, by such special Act, extended, limited or qualified, the corresponding provision of this Act shall be taken to be excepted, extended, limited or qualified in like manner.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
You still have the old nightmare of the special Act subse-

quently passed by a provincial legislature. Suppose you have an Act passed next year giving a railway company In the province of Nova Scotia seven years to complete its road. The road connects, let us say, with the Intercolonial Railway, and is connected at once, and then construction is started towards the Strait of Oanso, as might be the case with the road proposed to be constructed through the county of Halifax. What would be the effect of this section upon it ?
I think that in that case, we could apply section 4.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This Act would then apply to such a railway to the exclusion of inconsistent provincial legislation. Therefore, you will not by section 117 reduce the time from seven years to five.
We may have amended it so as to destroy the application, but otherwise it would.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In any event I suppose it is a very unlikely case.

Section agreed to.
On section 118, subsection (g) :
Erect and maintain all necessary and convenient buildings, stations, depots, wharfs, and fixtures, and construct, purchase and acquire stationary or locomotive engines, rolling stock and other apparatus necessary for the accommodation and use of the passengers, freight and business of the railway.
I propose to amend this section, in the first place, by placing the word ' construct ' at the beginning of the section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
lion. Mr. HAGGART. I see that the words in the existing law, ' carriages, wagons, boats and other machinery,' are struck out.

Yes. I propose also to insert in the first line of the subsection, after the word * convenient,' the word ' roads,' and, after the word ' wharfs,' in the second line of the subsection, the words 1 docks, elevators,' and to strike out the word ' fixtures ' and insert the words ' other structures.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Amendments agreed to.
Why not, instead of ' passengers, freight and business,' use the words ' traffic and business,' for ' traffic ' is defined in the interpretation clauses as covering passengers and freight ?
Very well. I move to strike out the words ' passengers, freight ' and insert the word ' traffic.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is no objection to the word ' business,' except that it seems to be covered by the other expression.
Better leave it there.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Why does not the hon. minister give the railway company power to buy carriages, wagons and boats for their business, to carry freight to and fro between the town and the station ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I do not think there is any doubt about their power to do that.
The expression ' other apparatus ' would cover that.

A good many of the railways do their own freighting in the cities.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	ANDCANALS. I think	they	do it through	independent organizations.

Some do it through subsidiary companies, but others do it direct.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I think it is covered by ' other apparatus.'
On section 118, subsection (i) :
Take, transport, carry and convey persons and goods on the railway, regulate the time and manner in which the same shall be transported, and the tolls to be charged therefor.

This will not give them compensation for carrying to and from the station. This is in line with leaving out the words ' carriages, wagons and boats for their business,' as given in the old Act. They are limited simply to tolls.
I do not think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think these two clauses were intended to be broad enough to cover the case I was mentioning, where a railway acts as its own freighter in a city it could buy carriages and wagons and could charge something more than a toll as compensation for the freightage.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. The subject was discussed very fully, and it was thought that the word ' tolls ' would be sufficient to cover it.
On section 118, subsection (j) :
Fell or remove any trees which stand within one hundred feet from the centre line of the railway, or which are liable to fall across any railway track.
I propose to ask the committee to strike out the words * the centre line ' and insert the words ' either side of the right of way.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
You give them
I power to cut trees within one hundred feet

from the side of the line of the road. Suppose the right of way is sixty-six feet wide, that would give them 133 feet instead of 100.
By the use of these words ' or which ' you may be going further than 100 feet from the right of way. Should we not describe some limit as to how far you will go ?
Go just as far as the tree may be high. If the tree is more than 100 feet high, they would have a right to cut it down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Look at the effect on the land owner. He would not know where the railway had a right to go, and he might get into complications in trying to prevent them from what he thought would be a trespass. It would be better to fix this a little clearer than to have the railway employees go into a man's field and take one isolated tree without being bound by any certain distance from the line of railway.
This has been the law for twenty years, and there have been no difficulties so far as we know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There have been troubles to my certain knowledge, and that is why I mention it. It would be better to say 150 feet if necessary.

I propose to restore a clause in the existing law and to make it subsection 2 of section 118 as follows :
Any company which has obtained from the Crown by way of subsidy or otherwise, in respect of the construction or operation of its railway, a right to any land or to an interest in land, has, and from the time of obtaining such rights has had, as incident to the exercise of its corporate powers, authority to acquire, sell or otherwise dispose of the same or any part or parts thereof ; and such company may convey the same, or any part or parts thereof, to any other company which has entered into any undertaking for the construction or operation, in whole or in part, of the railway in respect of which such land or interest in land was given ; and thereafter such other company shall have, in respect of such land or interest in land, the same authority as that of the company which has so conveyed it; and as to any lands given to the company by any corporation or other party as aid towards, or as consideration in whole or in part for, the construction or operation of the company's railway, either generally or with respect to the adoption of any particular route, or on any other account, the authority of the company and of any other company to which it may convey its right in any of the said lands shall be the same as if such lands had been obtained by the company from the Crown as aforesaid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If I understand the hon. minister rightly, this gives the company power to convey land to another company to be used for a similar purpose to that for which it was required by the company conveying it. It does not interfere with the purpose for which the land has
been expropriated. According to some opinions when land is not used for the purpose for which it is expropriated it reverts to the original owners.
Some opinions hold that it does revert altogether.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This gives the company which has expropriated land for railway purposes power to convey it to another railway company which has to use it for the particular purpose that the company which expropriated it intended to use it for.

It enables a company to dispose of its lands as freely as a private individual may. It cannot acquire, sell or dispose of lands that it has obtained for the purposes of the company except in a very limited way and under special conditions, but if it has received by way of bonus or grant an area of land from any source, it can deal with these lauds the same as a private individual can, and if there are any conditions attached to it, such as that a railway shall be constructed, the company may transfer these lands to another railway company and the other railway company is bound by the conditions and shall be entitled to exercise all the rights and powers the same as the original grantee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then it goes farther than I stated. Where a railway company receives a grant of land for the purpose of erecting a station in a particular part of the town it may, upon the non-user of the station, abandon the property, dispose of it absolutely to another person just the same as the original grantor could to the railway company or any other person.
No, it does not mean that. It is not applicable to any such case at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The trouble is that we cannot tell from looking at the amendment because we would have to look at the particular section which it amends and we have not that before us.
We will pass it and if the hon. gentleman sees anything about it that he would like to have altered he can call attention to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it would be desirable to let us see the original section and bring it up again.

There is no objection to that. Section allowed to stand.
